Sate

SAYT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To sate is to satisfy fully, especially an appetite or desire.

A single bowl of the warm stew was enough to sate even the hungriest hiker.

Worked Example

No amount of applause seemed able to sate the young performer's hunger for attention.

This wasn't ordinary satisfaction -- the desire ran so deep that nothing seemed to fully quench it, which is exactly what sate describes (or fails to, here).

How Sate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

satisfy

satisfy: fulfill a need, desire, or appetite

quench

quench: satisfy a strong desire, especially thirst

Antonyms

whet

whet: sharpen or awaken an appetite or desire

How Strong Is It? — please → sate → glut

please vs. sate

please vs. sate: Pleasing someone makes them happy in a general sense; sating them specifically fills an appetite or craving until nothing more is wanted.

glut vs. sate

glut vs. sate: Sate describes fully satisfying a desire; to glut someone goes further, filling it to the point of excess or discomfort.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Sate comes from Old English sadian, related to Latin satis, 'enough' -- the same ancient root behind the everyday word satisfy.

Use the root in a new word: satisfy

Use the root in a new word: satisfy: The same satis root gives us satisfy (satis- 'enough' + facere 'to make') and satiate, sate's own closely related cousin.

Word Choice

Sate is most often used for appetites, cravings, and curiosity -- physical or emotional hungers that are finally, fully satisfied.
